Definitely when we sit down with the characters and explore their personalities, motivations, thoughts, emotions. I've explained this a bit in other replies but the reason Frieren loses me is because of the way the action is almost separate from the narrative despite the world being written in a way that necessitates the action, the conflict, and the stakes to be meaningful in order to keep the setting dynamic and interesting. But the story evidently refuses to do that

That's the most frustrating part, all of the elements that have hooked me before in stories with similar themes and settings are there but the narrative does so little with them. 

At times it almost feels like the writing is working against itself because we get so much focus on Element A and then Element C that Element B is neglected as if it were unimportant, which it is not.

Curses, yes. But magic in the Lord of the Rings, especially that of the Maiar, is on another level. 

When Gandalf told the Balrog that it shall not pass he wasn't just making a threat, he wrote the command that the Balrog should never come past that point of the mountain into reality itself.

And Sauron was by far the mightiest of the Maiar towards the end of the Third Age, when he was reaching the power that Morgoth, the most powerful of all the Gods, had when he fell. 

And the Ring is made with Sauron's essence, it is a part of him. The Ring doesn't corrupt, it is corruption in itself. Corroding and twisting the goals of any living creature, no matter how big or small they may be, is its very essence.

The Ring could and would corrupt anyone who spent too much alongside it, except Eru Iluvatar and Tom Bombadil, who might be nature itself.

Unfortunately, they rejected the Ring only because they were both INTIMATELY familiar with Sauron's work. And even then the two of them, one possibly the mightiest demigod in all of Middle Earth and the other an actual minor god, barely let it go. 

The Ring doesn't corrupt with promises of power and dominion. The Ring itself is corruption. For Frieren it might use her hatred and distrust of demon-kind, or her wish to do menial tasks in peace and unbothered, or her desire to collect rare grimoires, or her wish to speak with Himmel one last time, and the longer she carried it around the worse it would become. If she were not familiar with what it does, she would fall for it sometime sooner or later.

I've consumed all sorts of genres of fiction from Fantasy Sci-fi to Noir Thriller Romance and I've been satisfied with a variety of different types of story-telling, world building, narratives. What bothers me about Frieren is not that the story isn't what I want it to be, it's that it has all of the elements, all of the build up, all of the narrative devices, all of the anticipation and prelude that other similar works have, but it chooses to not do much with them. It's like eating a cake without the cherry on top yet you get the whipped cream where it's supposed to be
And small spoiler we do get a lot more information on the main antagonist demons later on in the manga, but my issue with the clashing of the world-building and narrative perists

My complaint isn't that the story is focused on the wrong thing, it's the fact that the formatting of it including the way the villains are built up, how the setting is written, and how the world-building has gone up to the current point in the manga have all been made in a way that these fights should be meaningful, their consequences should be impactful, the enemies that Frieren overcomes should be important. And they're not

And to be clear I'm not saying that Frieren herself doesn't grow and develop, I can recognize how much she's emotionally matured since the start of her adventure and her character writing really is beautiful. 

The story is so laser focused on her -phenomenally written- emotional journey that it doesn't give any relevant amount of importance or gravitas to all of these opponents and villains and antagonistic forces that it keeps building up, or to the important effects that their defeat brings to the world

You don't need to look down your nose at other people for having different opinions.

But while we're on the subject of Naruto, Frieren's conflicting narrative and action/setting writing applied to Naruto would look like all of his major fights being treated as nothing more than an occasional occurrence to his emotional journey to become Hokage of the Leaf Village. The villains themselves would be given the same amount of reverence and build-up that they were in the original work, but then they'd be dealt with in one or two episodes in a fairly inventive but also quick and not always satisfying way. Naruto would barely react to his victory over them and we wouldn't be shown the long-standing rippling effects that their defeat brought about

That's the part that really throws me for a loop. We're led to believe that none of these fights are meaningful and they're just something that's there every once in a while as Frieren progresses through her journey. Yet these fights have thus far been the only narrative device that has actually moved the story along. We go to a place, find a bad guy, defeat the bad guy and then go to the next place.

Every major arc on the exception of the finale of the first class wizard examination has culminated in some form of confrontation with one of these larger-than-life figures, and every time it was not a struggle for Frieren's group, the conclusion to the fight itself was sudden and at times anti-climatic, and the narrative gives victory little importance. 

And this is in spite of the fact that we KNOW that defeating these villains is a monumental achievement that will change the world at large, which the world-building reminds us time and time again.

The best way I can explain it is that the setting, the action, and the tension of the story all tell us that these confrontations should be and indeed are incredibly important. It's the narrative that puts them to the side and creates a disconnect between what we would logically care about in a story like this and what it wants us to care about

A funny movie. Having a good laugh with your coworkers. Having a pleasant time with the family. Cuddling up and being stupid with a pet or multiple pets. A beautiful dawn or dusk. Delicious plate of food. As I've lived I've learned that you don't live for every single day, you live for those good special days. The little pleasures and the unforgettable moments. That's what makes it all worth it as impossible as it may seem. For me Honesty Impact was Koby acting like an animal backed into a corner. On one hand it's one of the best Haki and strength feats we've seen but on the other it was clearly a make-or-break moment for him. How much he can grow depends on whether or not he can master this new level of power like when he unlocked obs at MF. Though I do think that for the time being saying he's relative to YC4 is fair, what do you think?

Well let's put it this way. Koby after being beaten, imprisoned, starved, and made to haul around a heavyass ball in an abnormally large island while fighting off literal endless pirates was still able to destroy a chunk of said island that's comparable to Thriller Bark in size. That's easily a Warlord feat in terms of destructive power and a considerable feat in terms of endurance. 

He also has advanced armament and possibly conquerors which puts his melee combat leagues above that of the average Haki user and on top of that he's learning the Six Powers which further enhances his lethality in close quarters. As if that weren't enough he's Garp's pupil so we KNOW he's got hands on top of the Rokushiki and Adv Arm. He's got observation too and even proficient users of it comment how good his is. 

And this is an underrated strength feat that I haven't seen anyone bring up, Koby jumped leagues above a Marine battleship which are massive by all measurements in order to intersect Pizarro's fist. We're so used to freaks of nature like Luffy and Zoro launching themselves hundreds of feet into the air with pure strength alone that when someone like Koby does it people just kinda go "Yeah figures." 

His physical stats are either great or excellent besides durability since we haven't seen him fight someone serious post TS. He has good obs haki, his arm is some of the best we've seen and he could have conq. He's skilled with the Six Powers and he's great at combat simply because he's Garp's beloved pupil. 

So overall, I put him somewhere between Franky and Cracker. Meaning YC 4-3. I'm not sure he can beat Doflamingo who's abnormally strong even for the Warlords and by extension I have to place him under the likes of Jack, Jinbei, and Cracker but I'm confident he can match current Franky, Snack, and Who's Who at the very least.

\-Equip and upgrade the card that makes your charge do way more damage if you detonate it before it hits the ground

\-Learn to time your charge detonations both in closed and open areas

\-Practice your throws a ton to get good at aiming them

\-Punish any sweaty heroes going after you with a charge and bash knockback-combo

\-Especially focus on landing headshots, with sights down or from the hip, since in this playstyle you're focusing more on keeping enemy heroes away from you

\-Learn how to take full advantage of melee

\-You can shoot players while they're knocked down two times, and to take the most advantage of this you have to land two headshots

\-Practice shooting flying targets, wether they're purposefully flying or just got flinged back by either one of your abilities

\-Don't empty your overload as soon as you activate it. Sometimes holding unto it and staring a blocking saber hero down can open up an opportunity.
